sections.body_en:
It is explained in the Tosefta (Shevi'it 8:1) that when the Sages saw that there were people who picked too much fruit in Shevi'it, they stationed agents on their behalf at the entrances to the towns, and from anyone who brought a lot of fruit from the fields they would leave him food for three meals, and the rest of the fruit they would take and bring into the storehouse in the town in order to distribute it to the other people. And when the picking season of the common fruits came, and likewise of grapes and olives, the beit din would hire workers to pick them, and they pressed the grapes in winepresses to make wine from them, and ground the olives in the olive press to make oil from them. And of the fruit, the wine and the oil they would distribute on the eves of Shabbat to all the people of the town, to each according to the needs of his household.

This enactment was meant to prevent transgressors from taking large quantities of fruit of Shevi'it and trading in it. Apparently the enactment had a further aim: to supply fruit of Shevi'it to all equally. For since it is hard for the people of the town to go out each time to the fields to pick fruit for the needs of their households, the agents of the beit din would pick the fruit for everyone. And presumably the beit din paid the workers from the communal fund collected from the taxes of all the town's residents. The Ramban added (Vayikra 25:7): "This fruit, gathered into the 'otzar beit din', does not need removal", since the whole aim of removal is that the person in whose possession the fruit is should bring it out into the public domain, and the fruit in the 'otzar' is already designated for the whole public (see above 4:10).

Some say that the enactment of 'otzar beit din' is the way to keep Shevi'it without needing the 'heter mekhira'. And further, some say that this is the right way to keep Shevi'it in our time, because today, when it is customary to grow fruit in large orchards far from population centres, it does not pay for a person to travel to an orchard to pick five kilos for his household's consumption. Therefore picking and distributing the fruit through an 'otzar beit din' is the only way by which the public can enjoy the fruit of Shevi'it.

On the other hand, some argue that the words of the Tosefta on the enactment of 'otzar beit din' were not accepted as halakha, and therefore this enactment is not mentioned at all in the Jerusalem and Babylonian Talmuds. And the Rishonim too hardly mentioned it, because carrying it out involves various prohibitions.

As we will learn below, although there are good answers to most of the objections to 'otzar beit din', in practice it is not a comprehensive solution to the question of Shevi'it, and in many cases this solution requires transgressing prohibitions of Shevi'it.1

notes_en.en:
The Ramban in his commentary on the Torah (Vayikra 25:7), and after him the Rashbash (Responsa siman 258), are the only ones among the Rishonim who mentioned the Tosefta (Shevi'it 8:1) as an enactment of 'otzar beit din'. Other Rishonim did indeed mention the Tosefta, namely the Rash and the Rosh (Shevi'it 9:8), Tosafot Rid (Pesaḥim 51b, s.v. 've-natal'), Tosafot of R. Shimshon of Sens (Pesaḥim 53a), Tosafot of Rabbeinu Yehuda Sirleon (Avoda Zara 62b). But they brought it in order to prove that removal is renunciation of ownership, and not as the view of the Rambam, who holds that removal is destroying the fruit (above 4, note 10). But one can understand that they agree with what is explained in the Tosefta, that the beit din may appoint agents to pick the fruit for all the people of the town.
The Rambam did not mention the enactment of 'otzar beit din', and some learned from this that in his view it has no place, because it is contrary to the mitzva of release, as explained in the next halakha. And in their view the other Rishonim too, apart from the Ramban and the Rashbash, do not agree with the enactment of 'otzar beit din'. And so wrote Rash Sirillo (Yerushalmi 9:6), and explained that the Tosefta deals with fruit of the sixth year which the beit din declared ownerless for the benefit of the poor. But it seems more likely that the Rishonim who did not mention this enactment also agree with its principle, as explained in the next halakha. And they did not need to mention it because it was enacted for its generation, and if there is a need for it in the future, it will be put into operation again according to the conditions of time and place. And so wrote the Ḥazon Ish 11:7; 12:6. And in the view of Rav Yisraeli in Ḥavat Binyamin 3:98, this is one of the ways of keeping Shevi'it in our time. And in the view of Rav Ya'akov Ariel, this is the good way to keep Shevi'it in our days (Teḥumin 28).
In practice, the Badatz of the Ashkenazim and Ḥasidim in Jerusalem operated an 'otzar beit din' for the first time in the year 5670, on condition that no forbidden work be done in Shevi'it, and that the price of the fruit be lower than usual. And Maran Rav Kook agreed to make use of it as an addition to the 'heter mekhira', but held that on its own it is not enough to rely on (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 313-314, Mishpat Kohen 76). And Rav Herzog and Rav Frank preferred not to combine it with the 'heter mekhira'. And the 'Ḥazon Ish' held that this is the proper way to supply fruit in Shevi'it and sustain the farmers, and operated an otzar beit din in the years 5705 and 5712. And Rav Yisraeli continued in his way, and even led, from the year 5719, the track of 'otzar beit din' within the framework of the Chief Rabbinate. After him Rav Ya'akov Ariel and 'Makhon Ha-Torah ve-Ha-Aretz' continued. See the article of Rav Yehuda Amiḥai in 'Ha-Torah ve-Ha-Aretz', vol. 8, p. 169 onward. Rav Ze'ev Weitman in his book 'Le-Kerat Shemita Mamlakhtit bi-Medinat Yisrael' proposed expanding the enactment in such a way that all agriculture and the distribution of fruit and vegetables in supermarkets would be managed as agents of the beit din, as in all the years, with a certain reduction of the price; this on the assumption that the 'heter mekhira' was meant for a pressing situation and that it is preferable to rely on all possible leniencies rather than on the 'heter mekhira'. He did, however, write that this proposal must be put before the rabbis of Israel. In practice, he himself merited to improve the management of the 'heter mekhira' within the framework of the Chief Rabbinate.
On the other hand, Rav Yehoshua Ben Meir in his book 'Ma Nokhal ba-Shana ha-Shevi'it – Heter Mekhira o Otzar Beit Din' detailed all the serious problems of 'otzar beit din', among them the work done to sustain the fruit, and that the farmers who own the field manage everything in the manner of owners. He explains the position of our great teachers Maran Rav Kook of blessed memory and those who followed him, and concludes on p. 97 that it is not right to operate an 'otzar beit din' at all, and only after the fact may one eat its fruit. As will be explained below, although some of the objections can be answered, two serious problems still remain: (a) work for the sake of sustaining the fruit; (b) trade. The first problem can be solved through the work of non-Jews, but for the second problem there is no solution, except in special cases in which the payment for the fruit of the 'otzar' can be significantly reduced. All this will be explained below.

sections.body_en:
Some hold that the enactment of 'otzar beit din' was not accepted, because according to the enactment the agents of the beit din must pick the fruit of the whole field, whereas the Torah forbade picking in Shevi'it the fruit of the whole field in the way one picks in all the other years, as it is said (Vayikra 25:5): "and the grapes of your untended vine you shall not gather." In addition, according to the enactment the agents of the beit din prepare large quantities of wine and oil, and for this purpose press the grapes in winepresses and the olives in olive presses, whereas the Sages forbade this, and permitted pressing grapes and olives only in small vessels (above 3:3).

But it seems in practice that the prohibition is for an individual to pick all the fruit for himself, but the beit din, as agent of the public, may appoint workers to pick the whole crop for everyone, just as several people may hire one worker to go to the field and pick fruit for each one of them for his household's consumption. And likewise the prohibition of pressing grapes in winepresses and olives in olive presses applies only to an individual, of whom there is a concern that he will press large quantities there for trade, which is forbidden with fruit of Shevi'it; but the agents of the beit din may do so as agents of the people of the town.

However, the field owners and the agents of the beit din may not prevent people from coming to the fields to pick fruit for their households' consumption.2

Even when the fruit is finished from the field, the 'otzar' does not need to remove the fruit in its possession. Because, as we learned in practice, removal is distributing the fruit to all (above 4:10), and since the fruit in the hands of the 'otzar' is meant for the benefit of the whole public, it is as if it is already removed. Indeed, the representatives of the 'otzar' guard it, but this guarding is for the public, so that whoever wants can receive fruit while sharing in the expenses of handling it. However, one who took fruit from the 'otzar' is obliged to remove it from his home and declare it ownerless when it is finished from the fields. But since he helped the beit din and paid for handling it, it is fitting that after he declares it ownerless they help him to acquire it again (as explained above 4:11).3

notes_en.en:
As explained in the previous note, according to Rash Sirillo (Yerushalmi 9:6) even the agents of the beit din may not pick a lot of fruit and process it in the way of all the years. And so is the view of Rav Herzog, Pesakim U-Khetavim, vol. 3, 72, because there is no hint of this heter in the Rishonim and the poskim. And so wrote Rav Ben Meir in 'Ma Nokhal', pp. 44-50, and so he learned in the words of the Rambam. On the other hand, those who support the 'otzar' explained that even the Rishonim who did not mention the 'otzar' agree with its principles, because the prohibition of harvesting grapes and picking is in the manner of owners, but when agents of the public pick the fruit for the people of the town there is no prohibition in it. And so wrote Sefer Ha-Shemita, part 1, 3:3, by Rav Tykocinski; the Ḥazon Ish 11:7; 12:5-6. And so explained the Ḥavat Binyamin, vol. 3, siman 98, and Rav Yehuda Amiḥai in 'Ha-Torah ve-Ha-Aretz', vol. 8, p. 169 onward. And it seems that one may rely on their words, for the reason I wrote above: just as a neighbour may pick for his neighbours, so the beit din may appoint an agent to pick for more people. (And this in combination with the individual view of the Rash and the Rosh, who permit reaping a whole field that was declared ownerless, above 3, note 3.)
In 'Shemita Mamlakhtit' 15, note 5, he holds that the beit din may prevent people from picking fruit from the orchard, for the prohibition of guarding applies only to the owner. But he concludes that the beit din can make do with demanding of those who come to take fruit that they pay their share of the handling expenses. And see 'Ma Nokhal' by Rav Ben Meir, pp. 73-74. And in my humble opinion one is obliged to release the field to all, and therefore it is forbidden to prevent those who want to from picking fruit; but one may ask them to pay their share for the handling, and if they claim sincerely that they are not interested in it, one should not oblige them to pay (see Ketif Shevi'it 22:10; and above 3, notes 12-13).

However, according to the Rambam and those who follow him, who hold that removal is destroying the fruit from the world, even the 'otzar' may not keep the fruit in its possession after the time of removal arrives. But as we learned (above 4, note 10), it was ruled in halakha that removal is declaring the fruit ownerless for all, and since the fruit in the hands of the 'otzar' is designated for the whole public, it does not need to be removed. Indeed, from the outset, where possible, it is good to take the Rambam into account and finish eating the fruit of Shevi'it by the time of removal.

sections.body_en:
If 'otzar beit din' made do with picking the fruit and distributing it, it could be carried out according to most of the poskim. But in order for many good fruits to grow on the trees, so that it pays to pick them and transport them to consumers, it is usually necessary to carry out in the orchards many treatments of fertilising, spraying, pruning and many other operations. Because in modern agriculture each tree and bush yields a large and fine quantity of fruit, several times what was usual in the past, and without all these treatments the trees and bushes will grow fruit that is significantly fewer and smaller than usual. And then there will be a twofold problem: first, since the fruit will be smaller and less fine, most consumers will prefer not to take it. And even if they reduce its price greatly, they will still have difficulty finding people who want to pay for it. Second, since the fruit growing on the trees will be noticeably few, it will not pay to hire workers to pick it. And if they raise its price in order to pay the workers who picked it, they will find hardly anybody who wants to pay for it.

However, the supporters of 'otzar beit din', headed by the author of the 'Ḥazon Ish', introduced a new halakha, according to which all the kinds of work that were permitted for the sake of sustaining the tree are permitted also for the sake of the fruit on the tree. On this basis they permitted almost all kinds of work, so that the fruit would reach a level at which it pays to pick and market it.

But as we learned (2:2-3), this view is contrary to the course of the sugyot in the Gemara and the Rishonim, in which it is explained that all the kinds of work forbidden rabbinically are always forbidden, except in individual cases in which it is permitted to do them for the sake of sustaining the tree. Whereas according to this approach it follows that most kinds of work are permitted, except in cases where there is no need for them and one should avoid them. And so Maran Rav Kook of blessed memory ruled, that it is forbidden to do any act for the sake of sustaining the fruit. Not only that, but the prohibition in this is based on the cancelling of a Torah mitzva. For all that they said, that there are kinds of work forbidden rabbinically which are permitted for the sake of sustaining the trees, refers to work done in a temporary way at a time when there is a special need for it, for then there is no violation in it of the general mitzva to rest from field work. But when a person works in the field in a fixed way, as is needed to grow the fruit of the 'otzar beit din', even if he did only kinds of work not mentioned in the Torah, he cancels a positive mitzva from the Torah that commanded resting in Shevi'it.

However, this problem can be solved by hiring non-Jews to carry out all the work for the sake of growing the fruit (as explained above 5:9).4

notes_en.en:
Above 2:2-3, note 3, the permission for work to sustain the tree and the prohibition of improving it are explained. Plainly it is clear that it is forbidden to do work for the sake of sustaining the fruit. And the Ḥazon Ish (16:4; 21:14) introduced the new view that even for the sake of sustaining the fruit it is permitted to do work. And so wrote Rav Tykocinski (Sefer Ha-Shemita 4:2, note 5). And Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Ma'adanei Eretz 7; the Ma'amar Mordechai 3:8-9; and Shevitat Ha-Sadeh 6:5, note 5, also agreed with their view. The Ḥazon Ish 21:15 further held that pruning is forbidden from the Torah only with a vine, and his words are rejected on the basis of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim, as explained above 2:5, note 5.
In the Ḥavat Binyamin 3:98; 103, he holds that as agents of the beit din it is permitted to do work to sustain fruit that has already begun to grow on the trees. But it seems that even if we accept his reasoning, at most we could permit sustaining the fruit in a minimal way, but there is no heter to do the many kinds of work needed today so that they can market it within the framework of the 'otzar' in competition with other fruit. And so hold some of those who follow this approach. But the organisers of the 'otzarot' rely on a report from the Ḥazon Ish that he agreed to permit all the kinds of work whose prohibition is rabbinic, so that the fruit growing in Shevi'it would not be significantly harmed in its quantity and quality compared with what is usual in the other years (see Mishpetei Eretz 3, note 5).
For halakha, even though today the mitzva of Shevi'it is rabbinic, these heterim should not be accepted, for they are contrary to the whole course of the sugyot. First, because the main view in halakha is that no work at all is to be permitted for the sake of sustaining the fruit, as Maran Rav Kook wrote (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:5:16; 1:15:4; Kuntres Aḥaron 12; Mishpat Kohen 79). And so wrote Torat Ha-Shevi'it p. 43; Devar Ha-Shemita p. 58. And as I wrote above 2, note 3. Furthermore, above 2, note 1, it is explained that one who does the work of the field in his usual way of all the years, even though he did not do one of the four kinds of work, cancelled a positive mitzva from the Torah, as it is said (Vayikra 25:4-5): "But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a sabbath to the Lord… it shall be a year of solemn rest for the land" (Ramban, Vayikra 23:24; Ritva, Rosh Ha-Shana 32b). And Maran the Rav expanded on this (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:4; Kuntres Aḥaron 2:1; 7), and explained that so it is implied from the words of the Rambam. Similarly wrote the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 19:3. Indeed, one can argue that since Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic, one may rely on these lenient views. But beyond the fact that it is very hard to accept their reasoning, it is much more correct for halakha to remove the mitzva by a sale than to argue that one is keeping Shevi'it while cancelling the core of its mitzva, the resting, according to Maran Rav Kook and those who hold with him. And it seems that the supporters of the 'otzar' hold that the core of the shemita is distributing the fruit to all, and therefore in their view all the leniencies accompanying the 'otzar' can be accepted, since they fit this aim. But resting is the core of Shevi'it, as explained above 1:1, and therefore the extreme leniencies of the 'otzar' uproot the core of Shevi'it. Consequently it is much more correct for halakha to remove the obligation through the 'heter mekhira'. In addition, the 'heter mekhira' rests to a great extent on the views that hold that there is no obligation to keep Shevi'it in our time, and on the doubt about the years; therefore it is more correct for halakha to permit the work by a complete removal through a sale than to argue that one is keeping Shevi'it while in practice causing the teaching of Shevi'it to be forgotten through extreme leniencies that cancel the resting entirely, contrary to the course of the sugyot in the Gemara and the Rishonim.
However, if the work is done by non-Jews, there is no prohibition in it, for 'shevut de-shevut' with a prohibition that carries no death penalty is permitted (see above 5:9). And still this is not the resting spoken of in the Torah, as I wrote similarly in Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 9:11, that the whole heter of 'shevut de-shevut' is for a pressing situation, but one should not base the order of Shabbat on the work of a non-Jew as 'shevut de-shevut'. Therefore, when we return to keeping Shevi'it by Torah law, we will not be able to carry out all the work of the field through non-Jews, but only at times will we be able to make use of non-Jews, in the way of 'shevut de-shevut' on Shabbat.

sections.body_en:
With vegetables, which must be sown anew every year, there is a further problem, since it is forbidden to sow in Shevi'it. Therefore it was proposed that the 'otzar' hire the farmers to sow the vegetables in their fields before the start of the seventh year, and pick them in Shevi'it, and the representatives of the 'otzar' would collect payment from the public for the work the field owners did as their agents.

As we learned (above 3:4), according to the Rambam, all grain, legumes or vegetables that grow in Shevi'it in a Jew's field are forbidden to be eaten because of the decree on aftergrowths. But according to the Rash and the Rosh, the decree on aftergrowths does not apply to vegetables that began to grow in the sixth year, since at that time it is permitted to sow; however, since these vegetables are gathered in Shevi'it, the holiness of Shevi'it applies to them.

And so it seems in practice: since the decree on aftergrowths is rabbinic, one may from the outset rely on those who hold that whatever began to sprout before Shevi'it, since it was sown with full permission, is not subject to the decree on aftergrowths. In this way there is a solution for supplying vegetables for the first half of the seventh year, but not for the second half and the beginning of the eighth year.5

notes_en.en: See above 3, note 5, that according to the Rash and the Rosh, vegetables that began to grow in the sixth year and were gathered in Shevi'it are not subject to the prohibition of aftergrowths, but have the holiness of Shevi'it. And so is the view of Tosafot and the Ritva. And according to the Rambam (4:9-10; 4:12), the Semag, Rash Sirillo and the Mabit, whatever is gathered in Shevi'it is included in the prohibition of aftergrowths. Most of the Aḥaronim ruled according to the view of the Rash (Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan, Shabbat Ha-Aretz 4:3; Sefer Ha-Shemita; the Ḥazon Ish). Some indeed hold that even according to the lenient it must reach the stage of tithing in the sixth year (Minḥat Shlomo 1:49-50); but in practice, since the decree on aftergrowths is rabbinic, the halakha follows the lenient. And this in addition to the fact that their reasoning seems right.

sections.body_en:
As we learned, some want to avoid using the 'heter mekhira' and conduct all the agriculture in the Land within the framework of 'otzar beit din'. But since the Sages forbade taking fruit that has the holiness of Shevi'it outside the Land in Shevi'it, and about half of the agricultural produce is usually sold abroad, at first sight this problem has no solution.

Even so, the supporters of 'otzar beit din' hold that since this is a pressing situation and a great loss, because if for one year fruit is not exported the competitors will take its place and very great damage will be caused to the farmers, one may rely on various lines of reasoning and permit exporting the holy fruit of Shevi'it abroad, as explained in the note. And although in a pressing situation one may rely on these lines of reasoning, it is more correct to rely on the 'heter mekhira', on which one may rely in our time from the outset, whereas on these heterim one may rely only in a pressing situation.6

notes_en.en:
Above 4:12 the prohibition of taking fruit of Shevi'it outside the Land is explained, and the simple way to permit this is through the 'heter mekhira', for after the fields have been sold to a non-Jew the fruit no longer has holiness and it is permitted to take it abroad. But those who want not to rely on the 'heter mekhira' looked for strained ways to permit taking the fruit of the 'otzar beit din' abroad. Let us explain their reasoning. In the Mishna Shevi'it 6:5: "One may not take out… fruit of Shevi'it from the Land to outside the Land." And in Pesaḥim 52b a baraita is brought: "Our Rabbis taught: fruit that went out from the Land of Israel to outside the Land is removed wherever it is. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: it should return to its place and be removed." And Rav Safra decided that the halakha follows the first Tanna. And so ruled the Rambam (5:13) that it is forbidden to take fruit of Shevi'it abroad, and if one took it out, he removes it abroad (7:12). And the Rash inclined to this in his commentary on the Mishna. But Maran Rav Kook wrote in Shabbat Ha-Aretz, Kuntres Aḥaron 23, that it is possible that according to the first Tanna there is also no prohibition at all in taking them out, as the Rash wrote at the beginning of his commentary, and only because of the doubt did the Rambam and the Rash rule stringently (and similar to this he wrote in the Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 24, se'if katan 56). Therefore in a pressing situation one can say that according to the first Tanna, who is Rabbi, there is no prohibition in taking fruit of Shevi'it abroad, and the halakha follows Rabbi against his colleague; and so Rav Safra acted, as brought in Pesaḥim 52b. They further wrote to be lenient in a pressing situation on the basis of Tosafot in Pesaḥim 52b, s.v. 'Rav', that according to the first answer he permitted taking out for trade in permitted ways. Thus far. And although it is forbidden to trade in fruit of Shevi'it in large quantities, in their view, as explained below in halakha 6, when the trade is through an otzar beit din it is permitted.
A further side to the heter is based on what they inferred from the Tiferet Yisrael (Hilkheta Gevirta 6:5), that the whole basis of the prohibition is that the fruit will be abroad at the time of removal, and consequently there is no prohibition when one exports the fruit in such a way that it will be eaten by the time of removal, or exports it after the removal (and until after the time of removal it will be in the possession of the beit din and thereby exempt from removal). Another line of reasoning was raised: that the whole basis of the prohibition on taking the fruit out is so that the people of the Land of Israel will have fruit to live on (as an extension of the prohibition of taking out fruit that sustains life in all the years, as explained in Bava Batra 90b), but when the trees were planted in order to export their fruit for the livelihood of the residents of the Land, there is no concern. And so wrote R. Ḥayim Berlin. And some were lenient when it is clear that there are not enough people in the Land to eat all the fruit, and if they do not export it abroad it will go to waste (brought in Beit Ridbaz, Mishmeret Le-Ha-Bayit). A further strain: the main aim of exporting the fruit is to profit, and this is forbidden because of trade.
In practice, Rav Ya'akov Ariel proposed (Be-Ohalah Shel Torah, vol. 3, 8) that they sell the fruit from the beginning of its growth to a marketing agency of non-Jews from abroad, and so it will have no holiness, and this agency will also export the fruit. And since perhaps this sale is not effective in removing the holiness of the fruit, when possible they should export the fruit in such a way that it will not be abroad at the time of removal. And similarly Rav Ze'ev Weitman wrote (Shemita Mamlakhtit 16), but he preferred to do this through a state otzar beit din, which would sell the fruit to a marketing agency of non-Jews. He also discussed in chapter 17 the question of marketing to non-Jews, and concluded that there is no prohibition in itself in feeding non-Jews, but the fruit is meant first of all for Israel; and consequently when the trees were planted for export, and likewise when without export abroad and to non-Jews it would go to waste, it is permitted to export it and sell it to non-Jews. All the more so when this is done within the framework of a beit din that ensures there will be enough fruit for the Jews of the Land. (And see further Shabbat Ha-Aretz 5:13, with the expansions.) Nevertheless it seems that after all the strained arguments we have found in this law, the 'heter mekhira' is much more comfortable. And so wrote the Ma'amar Mordechai 13:47, that it is forbidden to export fruit abroad without a 'heter mekhira'.

sections.body_en:
The Torah forbade trading in fruit of Shevi'it in the way one trades in all the other years, as it is said (Vayikra 25:6): "And the sabbath of the land shall be for you for food", which the Sages explained: "for food and not for trade" (Avoda Zara 62a). Even when selling a little fruit, the Sages forbade selling by weight or by measure, or in fixed places in the market or in shops, as in the other years, so that it would be sold cheaply and people would remember that it is fruit of Shevi'it.

Therefore some hold that it is forbidden to sell the fruit of the 'otzar' in shops by measure or weight, and those who do so transgress the prohibition of trade in Shevi'it (above 4:6). And what was permitted in the Tosefta is distributing the fruit to all the people of the town free of charge, and presumably the wages of the workers who picked and brought the fruit were paid from the communal fund. In addition, since the payment is for the fruit, the money takes on the holiness of the fruit (as explained above 4:7), and there is a concern that many will stumble and treat the money as ordinary.

On the other hand, some hold that the prohibition of trade applies only to fruit owned by a particular person, where the payment is for the fruit itself. Whereas within the framework of the 'otzar' the fruit is not in the possession of a particular person but in the possession of the whole public, and the agents of the beit din organise the fruit so that the whole public can enjoy it. Consequently the payment is not for the fruit but for the work involved in handling the fruit and bringing it to the public, including the work of spraying, fertilising, pruning, picking, packing, transport, distribution and organisation. Therefore it is also permitted to measure the fruit, in order to know how much to pay for the work invested in bringing it to distribution. And therefore the holiness of Shevi'it also does not take hold of the money paid to the 'otzar', for the payment is not for the fruit itself but for handling it (see above 4:7).

Indeed it would be fitting for the fruit of the 'otzar' to be distributed in public places and not in shops meant for trade; but when this is hard to carry out, after the fact it can be distributed in shops, with a clear separation between it and the other fruit, so that it is evident that it is not among the products traded in the shop. And indeed from the outset it would be fitting to distribute it to Jews who will be careful to treat it with holiness as the halakha requires. But after the fact, just as one does not station guards in the fields to prevent Jews who are not careful about halakha, or non-Jews, from picking fruit of Shevi'it, so one need not prevent this in shops. But in shops where most of the customers are non-Jews, or Jews who may not treat it with holiness and may waste it, it is forbidden to distribute this fruit.

Some hold that the representatives of the 'otzar' may collect a payment equal to, or even slightly higher than, the price of ordinary fruit, because the cost of handling the fruit of Shevi'it is higher, for in Shevi'it some of the field work, such as pruning, must be done with a change that lengthens the workers' labour. In addition, the supervision of the fruit of the 'otzar' is more expensive, since more supervisors are needed to guide the farmers in the laws of work in Shevi'it, to set the prices of the fruit according to a calculation of the work invested in it, and to oversee the distribution of the fruit, which is done according to the instructions of the beit din.

For halakha it seems that only when the fruit of the 'otzar' is distributed for a price significantly lower than is usual in the market is there no prohibition of trade in it, for the low price expresses the fact that this is ownerless fruit, and the payment is for the trouble of preserving and distributing it. But when the price is close to the usual market price, it is trade. And therefore when it is possible to collect more, they collect more, and when it is not possible to collect more, they collect less. In practice, the batei din too try to make the prices of the fruit in their charge cheaper than the market price.7

notes_en.en:
The reasoning of those who forbid receiving payment for the fruit of the 'otzar' is that even if we accept the words of the Tosefta, nevertheless we have not heard of payment for the fruit. And so wrote at length Rav Ben Meir, 'Ma Nokhal', pp. 76-80. And some say that even if we permit receiving payment for the picking, packing and distribution, it is impossible to permit payment for the handling of the tree and the fruit. And so wrote Rav Ḥarlap (brought there), and the Minḥat Shlomo, vol. 3, 132:16-17. And Rav Eliyahu was concerned about all this, and therefore required arranging a 'heter mekhira' together with an otzar beit din (Ma'amar Mordechai 18:5, and siman 11).
On the other hand, those who permit hold that since the payment is for the handling and distribution of the fruit, there is no prohibition in it. And after the fact the distribution may be carried out in shops as well. And so wrote Rav Yisraeli in Ḥavat Binyamin 3:98; Rav Ya'akov Ariel in Teḥumin 28; Shevitat Ha-Sadeh 13:7, in the name of the Ḥazon Ish; and there 13:11; Mishpetei Eretz 13:5.
And in my humble opinion, the whole heter to sell fruit of Shevi'it, even within the framework of the 'otzar', depends on the fruit being significantly cheaper than the other fruit, as they said in the Mishna (8:3): "One may not sell fruit of Shevi'it by measure, nor by weight, nor by number…", and in the Yerushalmi there: "Why? So that it will be sold cheaply" (and see Yerushalmi Mo'ed Katan 2:3). And so wrote Rash Sirillo (Yerushalmi 7:3): "'And his son sells on his behalf' – for him, that is, in his place he sells in the market, for since he did not gather it and did not take trouble over it, he sells it cheaply." But when their price is around the market prices, or even slightly lower, there is a prohibition of trade in them (see above 4:6). For one must know that nothing has a "reasonable price" or a "true price"; rather all prices, including workers' wages, are set according to the rules of supply and demand, and this is the essence of trade. Therefore when there is no demand for a certain thing, its price falls, and consequently the wages of the workers in it are cut. And when there is great demand for a certain thing, its price rises, and so do the wages of its workers. And if we see that the prices of the fruit of the 'otzar' are close to the price of ordinary fruit, they were set according to the rules of trade.
In addition, if the prices are not cheap, the beit din is no longer of benefit to the public, and consequently the objections of those who forbid, because of the problem of picking and removal and the large scale of the trade, return to their place (above 2, notes 2-3). Similarly the Badatz of the rabbis of Jerusalem ruled in the year 5670 that the fruit must be cheaper than the other fruit ('Ha-Torah ve-Ha-Aretz', vol. 8, p. 184). And so wrote Shevitat Ha-Sadeh 13:9, note 9, that so ruled Rav Ovadia Yosef and Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv; for otherwise the public would say to the beit din managing the otzar: I sent you to set things right, not to make them crooked. Indeed Rav Weitman in 'Shemita Mamlakhtit' 18, notes 6-7, wrote that according to Rav Nissim Karelitz the 'otzar' may collect payment for its expenses even if they are higher than the price of ordinary fruit. And he explains that it is logical that its price would be higher, because of the additional costs of handling it. But in practice he wrote that from the outset it is right to reduce the prices of the fruit significantly.

sections.title_en: 7. The Problem of Trade and Prices
sections.body_en:
As we learned, the main condition for operating an 'otzar beit din' is that the payment for the fruit of the 'otzar' be significantly lower than the price of similar fruit sold in the market from the 'heter mekhira' or from fruit imported from abroad. But in practice the batei din have difficulty meeting this, and many times they are forced to charge a price higher than the market price in order to cover their costs. And here the beit din enters a dilemma: if it subsidises the prices of the fruit, it will find itself in debt and will not manage to pay wages to the farmers and marketers working as its agents. If it charges the cost price of the workers on its behalf, the prices of the fruit of the 'otzar' will rise, and consequently those buying it will become fewer, and again the beit din will have no money to pay the workers on its behalf.

It seems that according to the rules of economics and 'price theory' this problem has no solution. Just as a communist economy is less efficient than a capitalist economy, and its production costs are higher than the production costs in a capitalist economy, so the costs of the beit din will be higher than the costs of the free market. For it is free competition that causes the field owners and the marketers constantly to strive to make their work more efficient, in order to make the prices of the fruit as cheap as possible. And when management is entrusted to people who do not personally profit from efficiency and do not need to withstand competition in order to survive and profit, it is inevitable that the management of the work will be less efficient and its fruit prices will rise. And the larger and more complex the system the 'otzar' manages, the less efficient its work will be. However, if the 'otzar' focuses on a few responsible farmers, and markets the fruit directly to people who are ready to take trouble to receive the fruit of the 'otzar', it can distribute the fruit at a noticeably cheap price, and the idea of the 'otzar' will be realised.8

notes_en.en:
It is hard to explain 'price theory' briefly, but free competition, which is the essence of trade, together with the personal motive of the growers and marketers to profit, causes work to become more efficient and prices to fall. And every attempt to organise everything from above while removing competition and personal motive causes production and marketing costs to rise. Therefore naturally the fruit of the 'otzar' will be more expensive than other fruit. Every real solution to the problem turns the managers of the 'otzar' into ordinary producers and traders competing in the market with a personal motive, and consequently it is forbidden because of trade in Shevi'it. Only on a small scale, through especially responsible farmers, and within a simple framework of marketing, can prices be reduced significantly. And even this thanks to the goodwill of the distributors and consumers to take trouble over receiving the fruit. But within a wider framework, despite all the good intentions, Shevi'it after Shevi'it the managers of the otzarot learn the hard way the foundations of the free market and price theory, and are forced to make the fruit of the otzar more expensive than the usual price, and even this while absorbing losses (some of which they cover by obtaining government budgets). The conclusion that follows: it is impossible to organise the distribution of cheapened fruit of Shevi'it within the framework of 'otzar beit din'.
For example, at first it was decided that since the payment to the 'otzar' is for the work, and there is no difference in the cost of picking and transport between fruit picked at the beginning of the season and fruit picked in the middle or at the end of the season, the prices of the fruit would be fixed for the whole season. But when they acted so, great losses were caused to the 'otzar'. Therefore they were forced to rule that since the other fruit in the market is sold according to supply and demand, with the price high at the beginning of the season and then falling, it is preferable that the 'otzar' too adjust the payment for distributing the fruit to market prices, in such a way that it is always cheaper than the price of the other fruit, but not too cheap; for if it sells too cheaply at the beginning of the season it will come to considerable losses, and there is even a concern that people will trade in its fruit (Shemita Mamlakhtit 13, note 7; Shevitat Ha-Sadeh 13:9, note 9). But in this way too, naturally the reaction of the managers of the otzar to price fluctuations was slow and not efficient enough, and as a result losses were caused.
Similarly, if the farmers work as agents of the beit din, they must be paid in advance as employees, regardless of the success of the crop and the price that will be received for it; but in practice experience showed that when they acted so, they lost a fortune, for the farmers did not work with maximum efficiency. Therefore some batei din established that the farmers would be paid according to the return received when the fruit is distributed. In practice, since the beit din had no interest in obtaining the maximum price for the fruit, the payment to the farmers was very low, and then the farmers complained: if they are employees, they should be paid a fixed payment, and if they are self-employed, they should be allowed to profit according to the value of their fruit. But this is forbidden because of trade. Therefore Rav Weitman proposed (Shemita Mamlakhtit 13, note 7) that they adopt a method in which the farmers work for the beit din as contractors, and their wages are according to the quantity and quality of the fruit they grow, at a price reduced from the market price. In this way they have an interest in working efficiently in order to increase their profits; but here a tension arises between the farmers, who want to permit more kinds of work and receive higher payment, and the supervisors on behalf of the beit din. In addition, fruit prices are not stable, and therefore there is always an argument about what the usual price is and what counts as slightly cheaper than it. After that he proposed a more complex proposal (there 13, note 8). The general rule is that from all the issues the batei din needed to deal with (see Shemita Mamlakhtit chapters 13, 18, 19), a basic fact emerges: when the management of the work is done by the beit din, the work is less efficient, the costs rise and the fruit prices soar compared with market prices. The more the managers of the batei din succeed in finding more efficient solutions, the more they will be forced to be traders, contrary to halakha. And still they will lose, for part of the system does not work according to the rules of the free market. If they succeed in finding a perfect solution, it is a sign that they are acting as traders at every stage of production and marketing, and consequently everything is forbidden because of trade.
However, an 'otzar' that makes do with small volumes and simple ways of marketing, and relies on distributors ready to distribute the fruit on a half-volunteer basis, and on a public ready to take trouble to receive the fruit, will be able to reduce the prices of the fruit it manages significantly, and there will be no prohibition of trade in this. And still there is room to doubt whether it is worth taking all this trouble, when the 'heter mekhira' is well founded, whereas the framework of the 'otzar' requires the farmers to work in Shevi'it in order to grow the fruit, contrary to what emerges from the halakhic sugyot, as explained in halakha 3.

sections.title_en: 8. Otzar Beit Din Is No Solution
sections.body_en:
The conclusion that emerges from all this is that although one may be lenient in having the agents of the beit din pick all the fruit of the orchard and manage the sale of the fruit (above 2-3), there is no solution in using an otzar beit din to sustain agriculture and the farmers in Shevi'it. First, in order for the fruit grown within the framework of an otzar beit din to be fit for marketing, many kinds of work must be permitted, which in a temporary way can indeed be permitted for the sake of sustaining the trees, but must not be permitted for the sake of growing the fruit; and when they are done on a fixed basis, the basis of their prohibition is from the Torah (above halakha 3; and see the end of note 4).

Second, the whole basis of the heter of 'otzar beit din' is on condition that the fruit be distributed at a significantly cheap price; but the 'otzarot' can meet this only when it is a matter of especially responsible farmers who market their produce directly to organised communities, and the more the 'otzar' tries to run a larger system, the more the cost of the fruit will rise. If the price approaches the price of other fruit, it will be forbidden to market it because of the prohibition of trade. And even if the managers of the 'otzar' rely on the lenient in this, it is likely that the price of the fruit of the 'otzar' will be higher than the price of other fruit, and then no buyers will be found for the fruit.

This is in addition to the difficult problem of exporting fruit of Shevi'it abroad; although we have found a possibility of being lenient in this in a pressing situation, it is more correct to do so within the framework of the 'heter mekhira', on which one may rely in our time from the outset.

Now one can understand why Maran Rav Kook, and after him Rav Herzog and Rav Frank, found no advantage in handling the fruit of Shevi'it through an 'otzar beit din'. In addition, this solution not only does not bring us closer to keeping the mitzva, but even distances us from the right repair. For the main aim of Shevi'it is that the farmers rest from work, whereas within the framework of 'otzar beit din' they supposedly keep Shevi'it while working in their fields as in the other years, and perhaps more. Indeed, the supporters of the 'otzar' hold that the core of the shemita is distributing the fruit to all; but as we learned above (1:1), the core of Shevi'it is the resting.

Therefore it seems that a farmer who is deciding between working within the framework of the 'heter mekhira' and working within the framework of 'otzar beit din' should be instructed to work within the framework of the 'heter mekhira'.

As for the buyers: if the price of the fruit of the 'otzar' is significantly cheap, there is an enhancement in preferring it. And if it is equal in price to ordinary fruit, and all the more so if it is more expensive, the fruit of the 'heter mekhira' should be preferred, because of the prohibition of trade.9

notes_en.en: Maran Rav Kook, out of his great piety, tried to find a way to satisfy all the views, even those that reject the 'heter mekhira', and therefore he tried to find a solution in which, in addition to the sale, they would afterwards also declare the fruit ownerless and afterwards pick it. But for this it is necessary that from the outset, in the sale to the non-Jew, they make a condition that the Jewish hired worker may declare the fruit ownerless before it is picked (see Mishpat Kohen 66-67). He further proposed that one declare the fruit ownerless and hand it over to a beit din, and they would give him permission to harvest it and receive wages for the trouble and the equipment (there 76). However, he wrote that this is only as an extra measure, after the main heter is based on the sale, but the otzar solution on its own is not enough to rely on (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 314). And so is the view of the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rav Eliyahu, that one should not operate an otzar without a heter mekhira (Ma'amar Mordechai siman 21). But Rav Herzog (Ketavim U-Fesakim 3:72), Rav Uziel and Rav Frank saw in the use of otzar beit din not an advantage but a disadvantage, and held that one should not weaken the heter mekhira with a proposal that is not better than it. See on all this the article of Rav Amiḥai, 'Ha-Torah ve-Ha-Aretz' 8, pp. 169-211; Rav Ben Meir, 'Ma Nokhal', pp. 95-96.
